```{r helpers}
# Every number in the text comes from a table written by the project's code, through the
# functions below. Nothing is typed. A missing file or row prints as [missing: ...].
options(knitr.table.format = "pipe")   # pandoc wraps long pipe tables in LaTeX and Word
knitr::opts_chunk$set(out.width = "100%")   # figures fit the text width in every format
tbl_dir <- file.path("outputs", "tables")
fig_dir <- file.path("outputs", "figures")
rd <- function(f) {
  p <- file.path(tbl_dir, f)
  if (!file.exists(p)) return(NULL)
  utils::read.csv(p, check.names = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
miss <- function(what) paste0("[missing: ", what, "]")
f <- function(x, d = 2) ifelse(is.na(x), "n.i.", formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ","))
p_txt <- function(p) ifelse(is.na(p), "n.i.", ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", paste("=", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))))
stars <- function(p) ifelse(is.na(p), "", ifelse(p < 0.001, "\\*\\*\\*", ifelse(p < 0.01, "\\*\\*", ifelse(p < 0.05, "\\*", ifelse(p < 0.10, "\u2020", "")))))

nums <- rd("note_numbers.csv")
num  <- function(name) { v <- nums$value[nums$name == name]; if (length(v) == 1) v else miss(name) }
numv <- function(name) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(num(name)))

# T2: reproduction counts by model and data version
T2 <- rd("note_T2_classification.csv")
cls <- function(model, version, col) { x <- T2[T2$model == model & T2$version == version, col]; if (length(x) == 1) x else miss(paste(model, version, col)) }

# T3: Durbin-Watson and Breusch-Godfrey comparisons, summed over the rows selected
T3 <- rd("note_T3_dwbg.csv")
dwbg <- function(col, test = NULL, version = NULL, convention = NULL) {
  x <- T3
  if (!is.null(test)) x <- x[x$test == test, ]
  if (!is.null(version)) x <- x[x$version == version, ]
  if (!is.null(convention)) x <- x[x$convention == convention, ]
  sum(x[[col]])
}

# T7 (long): the expectation coefficient at each correction step. step = the row number ("0", "1", "1b",
# "1c", ..., "4c", ..., "7"), matched exactly against the column step_id, so "4" does not also pick "4c";
# contains = text that tells apart rows with the same number (step 2: "wild"/"block"; step 7: the variant).
T7 <- rd("note_T7_expectation_long.csv")
tf <- function(x) toupper(as.character(x)) %in% c("TRUE", "T")
t7 <- function(model, step, period, what = "cell", contains = NULL, d = 2) {
  id <- trimws(step)
  hit <- if ("step_id" %in% names(T7)) T7$step_id == id else startsWith(T7$step, step)
  x <- T7[T7$model == model & hit & T7$period == period, ]
  if (!is.null(contains)) x <- x[grepl(contains, x$step, fixed = TRUE), ]
  if (nrow(x) != 1) return(miss(paste(model, step, period, contains)))
  if ("applies" %in% names(x) && !tf(x$applies)) return("not applicable")
  switch(what, coef = f(x$coef, d), se = f(x$se, d), p = p_txt(x$p), stars = stars(x$p), sign = x$sign,
         cell = if (is.na(x$coef)) "not identified" else paste0(f(x$coef, d), stars(x$p), " (SE ", f(x$se, d), ")"))
}

# T8: pooled-model Wald tests
T8 <- rd("note_T8_pooled_tests.csv")
wt <- function(model, version, type, test, regimes, what = "full") {
  x <- T8[T8$model == model & T8$version == version & T8$type == type & grepl(test, T8$test, fixed = TRUE) & T8$regimes == regimes, ]
  if (nrow(x) != 1) return(miss(paste(model, version, type, test, regimes)))
  switch(what, p = p_txt(x$p_F), full = sprintf("*F*(%d, %d) = %s, *p* %s", as.integer(x$q), as.integer(x$df2), f(x$F, 2), p_txt(x$p_F)))
}

# T12: CPI checks; T13: Period 1 variation; T5: unit roots
T12 <- rd("note_T12_cpi_check.csv")
T13 <- rd("note_T13_period1.csv")
p1 <- function(version, col, d = 3) { x <- T13[T13$version == version, col]; if (length(x) == 1) f(x, d) else miss(paste(version, col)) }
tf <- function(x) toupper(as.character(x)) %in% c("TRUE", "T")

# Relabelling check (cell level) and bootstrap summaries
RL <- rd("corr_relabel.csv")
rl_se_only_miss <- function() {
  if (is.null(RL)) return(miss("corr_relabel.csv"))
  x <- RL[!tf(RL$stars_match_if_se), ]
  if (!nrow(x)) return("none")
  paste(sprintf("Model %s, Period %d, %s", x$model, x$period, x$term), collapse = "; ")
}
BT <- rd("corr_bootstrap.csv")
# s2c: bootstrap with a stage-2 constant; by default as in the analysis (W4-20: only on the corrected data,
# s2c_of() in code/R/corrections.R)
bt <- function(version, scheme, period, col, term = "DER_hathat", d = 2, s2c = version == "corrected") {
  B <- if ("stage2_const" %in% names(BT)) BT[tf(BT$stage2_const) == s2c, ] else BT
  x <- B[B$version == version & B$scheme == scheme & B$period == period & B$term == term, col]
  if (length(x) != 1) return(miss(paste(version, scheme, period, col)))
  if (col %in% c("p_boot", "p_naive")) p_txt(x) else if (is.numeric(x)) f(x, d) else x
}
bt_min_ok <- function() if (is.null(BT)) miss("corr_bootstrap.csv") else min(BT$n_ok)
sel <- rd("selected_inputs.csv")
sel_col <- function(what) if (is.null(sel)) miss("selected_inputs.csv") else sel$selected_column[toupper(sel$input) == what]

# Verification of the extracted appendix against original Tables 3.2-3.9 (Week 2)
V3 <- rd("verify_T3_summary.csv")

# Tables: every table is drawn with flextable (HTML, Word and PDF alike), with fixed column widths
# that add up to the text width, so wide tables fit the page. Tables 1a/1b come with a status file
# (R/P/N per reproduced cell, rules in W1-07): those cells are shaded green / yellow / red.
SHADE <- c(R = "#C6EFCE", P = "#FFEB9C", N = "#FFC7CE")
# Optional: widths = relative column widths (overrides the automatic ones); size = font size;
# left = columns aligned left (default: the first only); pad = space on each side of a cell (pt). In the
# PDF, flextable ignores cell padding, so pad is passed as the column gap (tabcolsep) and the widths are
# reduced by that gap, keeping the table inside the text width.
ftab <- function(d, digits = 3, status = NULL, width_in = 6.3, widths = NULL, size = NULL, left = 1L, pad = 2) {
  if (is.null(d)) return(miss("table"))
  d <- as.data.frame(d, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  d$line <- NULL
  for (v in names(d)) {
    x <- d[[v]]
    if (is.numeric(x)) x <- ifelse(is.na(x), "", ifelse(abs(x - round(x)) < 1e-12, formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ","),
                                                   formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)))
    x <- as.character(x); x[is.na(x)] <- ""
    d[[v]] <- x
  }
  labels <- gsub("_", " ", names(d))
  if (!is.null(status) || identical(names(d)[1], "row")) labels[1] <- " "
  labels <- sub(" (published|reproduced)$", "\n\\1", labels)          # two-line headers in Tables 1a/1b
  if (!requireNamespace("flextable", quietly = TRUE)) {
    names(d) <- labels
    return(knitr::kable(d, align = c("l", rep("c", ncol(d) - 1)), row.names = FALSE))
  }
  ft <- flextable::theme_booktabs(flextable::flextable(d))    # horizontal rules only, as in JCRE articles
  ft <- flextable::set_header_labels(ft, values = stats::setNames(as.list(labels), names(d)))
  if (!is.null(status))
    for (cl in intersect(setdiff(names(status), c("row", "line")), names(d)))
      for (k in names(SHADE)) {
        i <- which(status[[cl]] == k)
        if (length(i)) ft <- flextable::bg(ft, i = i, j = cl, bg = SHADE[[k]])
      }
  ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = setdiff(seq_len(ncol(d)), left), align = "center", part = "all")
  ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = left, align = "left", part = "all")
  ft <- flextable::fontsize(ft, size = if (!is.null(size)) size else if (ncol(d) > 7) 7.5 else 8.5, part = "all")
  ft <- flextable::padding(ft, padding.top = 1, padding.bottom = 1, padding.left = pad, padding.right = pad, part = "all")
  # widths in proportion to the longest entry of each column (header words included), within limits
  ew <- function(x) { u <- nchar(gsub("[^A-Z0-9_]", "", x)); nchar(x) + 0.4 * u }   # capitals and digits are wider
  longest <- function(v, h) max(ew(c(v, strsplit(h, "[ \n]")[[1]])), 3)
  w <- pmin(pmax(mapply(longest, d, labels), 4), 45)
  if (!is.null(status) || all(grepl("^P[1-4]", names(d)[-1])))          # period columns: equal widths
    w <- c(min(w[1], 22), rep(max(w[-1]), ncol(d) - 1))
  if (!is.null(widths)) w <- widths
  avail <- width_in - ncol(d) * 2 * pad / 72
  ft <- flextable::width(ft, j = seq_len(ncol(d)), width = avail * w / sum(w))
  flextable::set_table_properties(ft, layout = "fixed", opts_pdf = list(tabcolsep = pad))
}
ptab <- function(name, ...) {
  d <- rd(paste0(name, ".csv"))
  if (is.null(d)) return(miss(name))
  d[] <- lapply(d, as.character)
  ftab(d, status = rd(paste0(name, "_status.csv")), ...)
}

pnotes <- function(name) {
  n <- rd(paste0(name, "_notes.csv"))
  if (is.null(n)) return(invisible())
  cat(paste0("^", n$letter, "^ ", n$note, collapse = "  \n"), "\n")
}
# Figures: path relative to docs/ (where Quarto and LaTeX look for them); error = FALSE because
# knitr would otherwise check the path from the project root, where R's working directory is
fig <- function(file) knitr::include_graphics(file.path("..", fig_dir, file), rel_path = FALSE, error = FALSE)
hv <- num("headline_version")
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Du, Ge and Qiao [-@du2014] estimate how expectations about the renminbi (RMB)–US dollar exchange rate affected the accumulation of China's foreign exchange reserves (FER) between 2000 and 2011. They split the sample into four exchange-rate regimes and measure expectations in two ways: a forecast generated from a three-stage regression model (Model I) and the 12-month non-deliverable forward rate (NDF, Model II). **[YOUR READING: in two or three sentences, the article's central claim as stated in its abstract and conclusion, quoted or closely paraphrased, with page numbers.]**

The question matters because **[YOUR READING: why this relation mattered, for example reserve accumulation and sterilisation costs, "hot money" inflows under an expected appreciation, and the policy debate at the time. One paragraph, with two or three references.]**

This note is a replication in the sense of the *Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics*: it assesses the reliability of the article's claims. We do two things. First, we **reproduce** the published estimates from the data of the original document on which the article is based, which contains the full dataset and every test and estimation table (@sec-reproduction). Second, we **correct** twelve problems in the original analysis, one at a time, and show how each correction changes the estimated effect of expectations (Sections [-@sec-corrections] and [-@sec-effect]).

**Disclosure.** The author of this note is the first author of the original article. To prevent the replication from being steered towards a preferred result, every rule that selects data, specifications or classifications was written down, dated, *before* the estimates it governs were computed, and the code and results of each step were committed to git. These rules include which balance-of-payments series is used, which unit-root specification, which Model I specification counts as the reproduction, and when an estimate counts as reproduced. Each rule is recorded, with the options considered and the evidence, in a numbered decision log, which Appendix A lists. **[W1-09: the log is kept off the public repository; state whether a cleaned version is published with the package or is available on request.]** All code and all public data are available at **[REPOSITORY URL]**; the only inputs that cannot be redistributed are the original document and the Wind NDF series (@sec-availability). The co-authors of the original study were informed of this replication on **[DATE]**. **[CONFIRM OR EDIT]**

@sec-original describes the original study, @sec-data the data, @sec-reproduction the reproduction, @sec-corrections the corrections, and @sec-effect their effect on the conclusions. @sec-availability explains how to reproduce every result, and @sec-conclusion concludes.

# The original study {#sec-original}

## Models

The article estimates two models of the monthly change in reserves, $\Delta FER_t$, separately in four periods. **Model I** builds an expected change of the exchange rate in three stages. Stage 1 regresses the change of the exchange rate (RMB per USD) on fundamentals:

$$
\Delta ER_t = b_0 + b_1\,\Delta BOP_t + b_2\,\Delta i_t + b_3\,\Delta \pi_t + b_4\,\Delta GDP_t + x_t .
$$ {#eq-stage1}

Stage 2 projects the stage-1 result on its own lags, without a constant:

$$
\widehat{\Delta ER}_t = \sum_{s=1}^{j} a_s\,\widehat{\Delta ER}_{t-s} + e_t ,
$$ {#eq-stage2}

and stage 3 uses the fitted value $\widehat{\widehat{\Delta ER}}_t$ as the expectation:

$$
\Delta FER_t = \tau_0 + \tau_1\,\widehat{\widehat{\Delta ER}}_t + \tau_2\,\Delta NX_t + \tau_3\,\Delta FDB_t + \tau_4\,\Delta FDI_t + y_t .
$$ {#eq-stage3}

**Model II** replaces the generated expectation by the observed 12-month NDF:

$$
\Delta FER_t = g_0 + g_1\,\Delta NDF_t + g_2\,\Delta GDP_t + g_3\,\Delta NX_t + g_4\,\Delta FDB_t + g_5\,\Delta FDI_t + w_t .
$$ {#eq-model2}

The variables are defined in @tbl-variables. In the original document, the regressions of Periods 1 and 3 have AR(1) errors (ARIMA(1,1,0)) and those of Periods 2 and 4 are estimated by OLS. The periods follow the exchange-rate regime (@tbl-periods).

```{r}

                        Months = sapply(PERIODS$period, function(p) sum(in_period(SAMPLE_MONTHS, p)))), width_in = 4)
```

All data and all reproduction targets are read by code from the original document; nothing is transcribed by hand. Appendix I of the original document supplies nine monthly variables for the 144 months from January 2000 to December 2011 (@tbl-variables). ## Inputs not in the original appendix

Two regressors are not in the appendix and were collected anew, and price data were added for the corrections (@tbl-sources; @data_safe; @data_wind; @data_imf; @data_fred; @data_nbs).

- **Balance of payments.** The quarterly current account (SAFE, BPM6 presentation) is converted to months. Of three candidate conversions (quarterly value held, divided by three, year-to-date), the one used, `r sel_col("BOP")`, was chosen by a rule fixed before any Model I estimate. The rule combines the distance to the original unit-root statistic and to the four stage-1 Durbin–Watson statistics (W2-01, W2-10, W2-12).^[The original document predates SAFE's BPM6 presentation and probably used BPM5 data, so a residual mismatch may reflect the accounting standard rather than the method.]
- **NDF.** The 12-month USD/CNY NDF is the only Wind tenor that covers 2000–2011. Month-end and month-average versions of the daily series were compared with the original unit-root statistic before Model II was estimated; the version used is `r sel_col("NDF")` (W2-06, W2-10).
- **Consumer prices.** For the deflator correction (@sec-deflator), a fixed-base consumer price index for China was taken from the IMF data portal and cross-checked against FRED (OECD data). The NBS published year-on-year index (same month of the previous year = 100) was used to identify the original study's inflation series (W4-05, W4-14).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sources
#| tbl-cap: "Data sources. Coverage: first and last observation in the file as downloaded. Layer rep: used in the analysis; check: used only to verify another series. Source: data/metadata/source_ledger.csv of the replication package."
s <- rd("note_T9_sources.csv")
# Layout only; every value is the ledger's. Coverage start and end share one column, underscores
# become spaces, and long codes get break points (a space after each comma; a line break after the
# last "/"), so that every entry wraps inside its column.
brk <- function(x) {
  x <- gsub(",(?=\\S)", ", ", x, perl = TRUE)
  ifelse(nchar(x) > 16 & !grepl(" ", x), sub("/(?=[^/]*$)", "/\n", x, perl = TRUE), x)
}
# A long path inside a sentence (no spaces) gets a line break after its middle "/".
brk_words <- function(x) vapply(strsplit(x, " ", fixed = TRUE), function(w) {
  long <- nchar(w) > 16 & grepl("/.", w)
  w[long] <- vapply(w[long], function(t) {
    pos <- gregexpr("/", t)[[1]]; pos <- pos[pos < nchar(t)]
    p <- pos[which.min(abs(pos - nchar(t) / 2))]
    paste0(substr(t, 1, p), "\n", substr(t, p + 1, nchar(t)))
  }, "")
  paste(w, collapse = " ")
}, "")
ftab(data.frame(Series = s$series_name, Provider = s$provider, Code = brk(s$series_key_or_code),
                Frequency = s$frequency, Coverage = paste0(s$coverage_start, " to\n", s$coverage_end),
                Method = gsub("_", " ", s$acquisition_method), Layer = s$layer,
                Licence_or_access = brk_words(s$license_or_access_restriction)),
     widths = c(1.0, 0.98, 1.36, 0.6, 0.78, 0.72, 0.36, 0.9), size = 7.5, left = 1:8, pad = 3)
```

# Reproduction {#sec-reproduction}

## Procedure

The reproduction follows rules fixed before estimation. Because the original document does not fully document Model I, all twelve combinations of its undocumented choices were estimated. These choices are whether stage 2 projects the stage-1 fitted values or the observed exchange rate, the number of lags (one to three), and whether the variables are used as published or divided by $\pi/100$, as the article states. The combination that reproduces most published cells was then named the headline (W3-02). Each estimate is classified on its sign and star level only (W1-07), with the meanings of the marks taken from the notes of the original tables and significance meaning *p* < 0.10. An estimate is **reproduced** if it has the same sign and the same star level as the published one, or if both are insignificant; **partially reproduced** if both are significant with the same sign but a different star level; and **not reproduced** if significance flips, or if the signs differ and either estimate is significant. Magnitude, measured as the gap in published standard errors, is reported but does not affect the class. First differences are taken on the whole 2000–2011 series (the "`r num("primary_convention")`" convention, W3-01); differencing within each period is reported as a sensitivity check.

## Unit-root tests

The article reports augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) tests; the original tables report DF-GLS tests [@elliott1996]. The original document does not state its lag rule. The specification that best reproduces the original statistics of the eight appendix variables was selected and then fixed (W2-02, W2-09). @tbl-unitroot shows the original statistics, our DF-GLS statistics and the ADF statistics at the same lag. DF-GLS and ADF agree on rejection at 5% in `r num("unitroot_agree")` of `r num("unitroot_n")` series. **[YOUR READING: how close our DF-GLS statistics are to the original study's (compare the first two columns), and whether any stationarity judgement differs.]**

## Estimates

The headline Model I specification uses the `r num("headline_spec")` stage-2 regressor with `r num("headline_lag")` lag(s) on `r num("headline_version")` data. It reproduces `r num("headline_reproduced")` of the `r num("headline_n_cells")` Model I cells; `r num("headline_partially")` are partially reproduced and `r num("headline_not_reproduced")` not reproduced. The ranking among the `r num("n_model_I_combinations")` combinations was decided by `r num("headline_decided_by")` (W3-07). For Model II on `r hv` data, `r cls("II", hv, "reproduced")` of `r cls("II", hv, "n_cells")` cells are reproduced (W3-08). Because two insignificant estimates count as reproduced whatever their size, the counts rest largely on such cells (W3-14): of the reproduced Model I cells, `r num("headline_reproduced_both_insignificant")` are insignificant in both the original and our estimates, and `r num("headline_reproduced_within_one_se")` lie within one published standard error of the published value; for Model II, `r cls("II", hv, "reproduced_both_insignificant")` and `r cls("II", hv, "reproduced_within_one_se")`. Tables [-@tbl-repro-a] and [-@tbl-repro-b] (Tables 4.9 and 4.10 in the original document; Table 4 in the article) set the published and the reproduced estimates side by side, and @fig-gap shows each gap in units of the published standard error.

Over all tables, data versions and conventions, `r num("dwbg_within_print")` of `r num("dwbg_n")` statistics agree with the printed values to the printed decimals, and `r num("dwbg_same_decision")` of `r num("dwbg_n")` test decisions agree (W3-12). # Corrections {#sec-corrections}

We take the twelve problems listed in the replication plan one at a time. For each, we state what the original did, why that is a problem, what we do instead, and what changes. The data and model changes are cumulative, and we assess their combined effect in @sec-effect.

## Standard errors labelled as t-statistics

The article describes the numbers in parentheses below each coefficient as t-statistics. The significance marks printed in the same table allow a direct test. If the parentheses held t-statistics, the marks would follow from those numbers; if they held standard errors, the marks would follow from the ratio of coefficient to parenthesis. Read as standard errors, the parentheses reproduce the printed marks in `r num("relabel_match_se")` of `r num("relabel_n")` cells (`r round(100 * numv("relabel_match_se") / numv("relabel_n"))`%); read as t-statistics, in `r num("relabel_match_t")` (`r round(100 * numv("relabel_match_t") / numv("relabel_n"))`%). The cells where the standard-error reading does not reproduce the marks are: `r rl_se_only_miss()`. **[YOUR READING: what the numbers in parentheses are, and whether the non-matching cells lie near a significance threshold (corr_relabel.csv, column implied_t_if_se).]** Throughout this note, the parentheses of the published tables are treated as standard errors.

## Units: level coefficients and log differences

All variables of @eq-stage1 to @eq-model2 are first differences of *levels*, so each coefficient is measured in the units of the variables in @tbl-variables, for example reserves per unit change of the exchange rate. **[YOUR READING: quote the article's percentage interpretation of a coefficient, with page, and state why a level coefficient cannot be read as a percentage.]** To give the coefficients a unit-free reading, all models were re-estimated with log differences of the strictly positive series (FER, the exchange rate, the NDF, GDP, FDB and FDI). The expectation coefficient then is an elasticity; net exports, the balance of payments, inflation and the interest rate stay in level differences (row 6 of Tables [-@tbl-steps-1] and [-@tbl-steps-2]).

## Sign convention

Both expectation measures are quoted in RMB per US dollar, so a rise is an expected *depreciation* of the RMB. A positive coefficient therefore means that reserves grow faster when a depreciation is expected, and a negative one that they grow faster when an appreciation is expected. **[YOUR READING: how the article describes the sign in its abstract and conclusion, and whether that description matches this convention. Use the Period 4 Model II coefficient: published sign from @tbl-repro-b.]**

## Generated regressors

In Model I, the stage-3 regressor is estimated in stages 1 and 2. The conventional stage-3 standard errors treat it as data and so ignore the sampling variation of the earlier stages [@pagan1984; @murphy1985]. A bootstrap of the whole three-stage chain includes that variation. Stages 1 to 3 are re-estimated in each of `r num("boot_B")` replications, with seed `r num("boot_seed")` (W4-01). The primary scheme is a wild bootstrap [@mammen1993; @davidson2008]: the residuals of stage 1 and the innovations of stage 3 are multiplied by the same Rademacher draw in each month, which preserves their correlation, and the AR(1) errors of Periods 1 and 3 are rebuilt from the sign-flipped innovations. A moving-block bootstrap within periods [@kunsch1989] is reported as a check. Every coefficient was estimated in at least `r bt_min_ok()` of `r num("boot_B")` replications.

For the headline specification on `r hv` data, the ratio of the bootstrap to the conventional standard error of the expectation coefficient is, by period: `r paste(sapply(1:4, function(p) paste0("Period ", p, " ", bt(hv, "wild", p, "se_ratio"))), collapse = ", ")` (wild) and `r paste(sapply(1:4, function(p) paste0("Period ", p, " ", bt(hv, "block", p, "se_ratio"))), collapse = ", ")` (block). @fig-ci compares the intervals, and @fig-draws shows the bootstrap distributions. **[YOUR READING: whether the conventional standard errors understate or overstate the uncertainty, and whether any significance mark changes (row 2 of @tbl-steps-1).]**

```{r}
#| label: fig-ci
#| fig-cap: "Expectation coefficient of Model I by period: 95% intervals from the conventional standard error, the wild and the block bootstrap (percentile), and the pooled model with Newey-West standard errors. Headline specification. Source: own estimates."
fig("fig2_expectation_ci.png")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-draws
#| fig-cap: "Wild-bootstrap distribution of the Model I expectation coefficient by period. Solid line: point estimate; dashed lines: conventional 95% interval. Source: own estimates."
fig("fig3_bootstrap_draws.png")
```

## Stage-2 constant {#sec-stage2-const}

**[WRITE (W4-20; companion 1.2): declare this as a correction outside the replication plan. Stage 2 (@eq-stage2) has no constant, so the forecast of the exchange-rate change has mean zero; in the managed-appreciation periods the change has a drift, which the lag coefficients then absorb (omitted-intercept bias). We add a constant to stage 2 on the corrected data (row 4c of @tbl-steps-1); for Model I, the bootstrap, the log-difference and the pooled rows on the corrected data build on it. Model II has no stage 2. Effect, from @tbl-steps-1, rows 4 and 4c: Period 2 `r t7("I", "4", 2)` and `r t7("I", "4c", 2)`; Period 3 `r t7("I", "4", 3)` and `r t7("I", "4c", 3)`; Period 4 `r t7("I", "4", 4)` and `r t7("I", "4c", 4)`. Your reading of the change.]**

## Year-to-date GDP

In the appendix, the GDP of every month of a quarter is the cumulative GDP of the year to date. Its first difference is therefore zero in two months of each quarter, positive at each quarter start, and strongly negative every January, when the cumulation restarts. This January fall is an accounting artefact that enters both models as a regressor. The correction replaces it by discrete quarterly GDP (the difference of consecutive year-to-date values), held in each month of the quarter (W4-05). The code first verifies that the appendix value is constant within every quarter. The effect is shown in row 3 of @tbl-steps-1 and @tbl-steps-2, to be compared with row 1b, the reproduction on the same (raw) data.

## Deflator {#sec-deflator}

The article divides every variable by $\pi/100$. Here $\pi$ is the consumer price index with the same month of the previous year = 100, a year-on-year growth factor $P_t/P_{t-12}$ rather than a price level. Dividing by it gives $X_t P_{t-12}/P_t$: the real value multiplied by last year's price level, not a real series. The correction divides the value variables (FER, GDP, net exports, FDI, external debt and the balance of payments) by a fixed-base consumer price index, rebased to 2000 = 100, from the IMF. The exchange rate and the NDF are not deflated: they are prices of one currency in another, and a real exchange rate would require both countries' price levels (W4-05).^[The US-dollar variables are thereby deflated by China's consumer prices, which measures their purchasing power over Chinese goods.]

We check the price data in two ways (@tbl-cpi and @fig-cpi). First, we compare the original $\pi$ with the same-month year-on-year index published by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS): `r num("cpi_pi_nbs_within_print")` of `r num("cpi_pi_n")` months agree within the printed decimals, with a largest gap of `r num("cpi_pi_nbs_max_abs_gap")` points (W4-14). **[YOUR READING: what this comparison shows about the source of the original $\pi$.]** Second, the year-on-year rates implied by the IMF index agree with the published ones within the printed decimals in `r num("cpi_nbs_imf_within_print")` of `r num("cpi_pi_n")` months (largest gap `r num("cpi_nbs_imf_max_abs_gap")` points).^[We compared the FRED series with the IMF's in the same way (largest year-on-year gap `r num("cpi_imf_fred_max_abs_gap")`). **[YOUR READING: whether FRED is an independent measure or the same index, and therefore what it confirms.]**] **[YOUR READING: from @fig-cpi, where the gaps between the published and the index-implied rates lie in time. "Our interpretation suggests ..." (for example the NBS basket changes; mark as a hypothesis).]**

```{r}

#| tbl-cap: "Consumer-price checks, 2000-2011. Within print: gap no larger than half a unit of the last decimal printed in the original document. Source: original Appendix I; IMF; FRED; NBS; own calculations."
ftab(T12, digits = 4)
```

## Period 1: exchange-rate variation

From January 2000 to June 2005 the RMB was pegged to the US dollar, and the appendix exchange rate is constant (standard deviation `r p1("raw", "sd_ER_level")` on raw data). Its change is zero, so no expectation effect can be estimated from it: the coefficient is not identified (W3-10). In the article's deflated data the exchange rate varies (standard deviation `r p1("deflated", "sd_ER_level")`), and that variation comes from the deflator: the $R^2$ of the deflated exchange-rate change on the change of $\pi$ is `r p1("deflated", "r2_DER_on_Dpi")` (@tbl-period1). A Period 1 "expectation effect" estimated on deflated data is therefore an effect of inflation. With the exchange rate undeflated (the corrected data), the Period 1 coefficient is reported as not identified.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-period1
#| tbl-cap: "Period 1: variation of the exchange rate, its change, and the stage-3 expectation term, by data version. Source: own calculations."
ftab(T13, digits = 4)
```

## Unit-root test label

The article reports ADF tests; the original study ran DF-GLS tests. @tbl-unitroot reports both at the same lag, and they agree on rejection in `r num("unitroot_agree")` of `r num("unitroot_n")` series. This correction relabels the tests and changes no conclusion that depends on them. **[CONFIRM from @tbl-unitroot.]**

## Chow tests, correctly specified

The classic Chow test [@chow1960] assumes equal error variances in the two regimes and no autocorrelation. Both assumptions are doubtful with monthly data across exchange-rate regimes. The corrected test estimates one regression over 2000–2011 in which every coefficient is regime-specific (@sec-pooled), and tests the equality of all coefficients of two adjacent regimes with a Wald test based on Newey–West standard errors (last column of @tbl-chow; @tbl-pooled). For the corrected data, Model I, the tests give: regimes 1–2, `r wt("I", "corrected", "full", "robust Chow", "1-2")`; regimes 2–3, `r wt("I", "corrected", "full", "robust Chow", "2-3")`; regimes 3–4, `r wt("I", "corrected", "full", "robust Chow", "3-4")`. For Model II, in the same order: `r wt("II", "corrected", "full", "robust Chow", "1-2")`; `r wt("II", "corrected", "full", "robust Chow", "2-3")`; `r wt("II", "corrected", "full", "robust Chow", "3-4")`. **[YOUR READING: whether the regime split of the original is supported, pair by pair.]**

## Period 2: pooled model with regime interactions {#sec-pooled}

Period 2 has about a year of monthly observations and five or six regressors, leaving very few residual degrees of freedom. Following the replication plan, the four periods are pooled in one regression with regime-specific constants. In the *full* variant every coefficient is regime-specific, which gives the same point estimates as the separate regressions but one set of standard errors for the whole sample. In the *expectation-only* variant only the constant and the expectation term are regime-specific and the controls are common (W4-02). Standard errors are Newey–West, with a lag of `r num("nw_lag_rule")` [@newey1987; @newey1994] (W4-03).

The expectation-only variant is valid only if the controls have the same effect in every regime. The Wald test of that restriction in the full model gives `r wt("I", "corrected", "full", "controls equal", "1-2-3-4")` for Model I and `r wt("II", "corrected", "full", "controls equal", "1-2-3-4")` for Model II (corrected data). The test that the expectation coefficient is the same in all regimes gives `r wt("I", "corrected", "full", "expectation equal", "1-2-3-4")` (Model I) and `r wt("II", "corrected", "full", "expectation equal", "1-2-3-4")` (Model II). **[YOUR READING: whether the equal-controls restriction is rejected, and therefore which of the two pooled variants is the appropriate one; then what the pooled model says about Period 2.]**

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pooled
#| tbl-cap: "Pooled models, 2000-2011, with regime interactions and Newey-West standard errors; corrected data. Source: own estimates."
ptab("paper_T4")
```

```{r}
#| results: asis
pnotes("paper_T4")
```

# Reproducibility and data availability {#sec-availability}

Every result in this note is produced by the code in the replication package, **[REPOSITORY URL]**, at commit `r num("git_commit")`, with `r num("r_version")` and the package versions recorded in `renv.lock`; the tables and figures were generated on `r num("date_outputs")`. The code starts from the raw files and runs in a fixed order; each script writes a run log. The bootstrap uses a fixed seed, so reruns give identical draws. **[CONFIRM from two 08_corrections logs: a rerun reproduced every estimate and bootstrap standard error.]**^[Python collects and registers the data; R estimates. Each script writes a run log to `outputs/logs/`.]

Public data (SAFE, IMF, FRED, NBS) are included in the package with their download dates and checksums (@tbl-sources). Two inputs cannot be redistributed. The original document is unpublished, and its reproduction targets (the numbers of its tables) are **[included / withheld; W4-08]**. The Wind NDF series is proprietary and is required to build the analysis panel: without it, the first estimation script (`01_import_verify.R`) stops, and no estimate can be reproduced (W4-23). A reader with Wind access can export the series using the code in @tbl-sources, register it with `register_wind.py`, and run the package unchanged.
